What still works without it: everything about plotting and exporting, and .arrow, .csv, .ipc, .parquet, .tsv for import.

topics.title: It is slow
topics.keywords: slow lag freeze hang performance waiting stuck unresponsive speed up
topics.body:
First, is it busy or is it stuck? The busy overlay names the job it is waiting for, and the job can be cancelled. The render badge means a full-resolution render is in progress and the preview on screen is deliberately the fast version.

Then, in order of how often it is the answer:

1. Field detail is too high. A contour or surface over scattered points is usually the slowest thing here, and the cost is quadratic - halving the detail is a quarter of the work. Turn it down until the contours start changing shape, then back up one step.

2. Too many points. Work out the figure on a subset with a SQL query, then run it on everything once.

3. The estimator is expensive. Kriging and the radial basis functions do a global solve. Inverse distance or Delaunay linear over the same points is a different order of cost.

4. The full-resolution render is set to run on every change. Options ▸ Full-resolution render, and Ask above sets the threshold past which it asks first.

Not usually the problem: the renderer. Switching to the GPU renderer helps a million-point cloud and does nothing at all for a slow field estimate, which is CPU work either way.

topics.title: The exported figure does not look like the screen
topics.keywords: export different wrong looks size text small background blurry mismatch changed
topics.body:
This is usually working as intended, and the reason is worth understanding.

The text is a different size. A publication profile re-renders the figure at the publisher's measurements, with text in points at final size. On a 89 mm figure with 6 pt text, the labels look large relative to the figure on screen and are correct in print. Set the profile and trust it rather than adjusting sizes by eye. See Why a profile re-renders.

The background is dark. The figure background is exported; the interface theme is not. If your figure came out dark, the figure background is dark. See Interface theme and figure background.

The grid has gone. Several publication profiles turn the grid off, because most publishers prefer it that way.

It is blurry in the document. You exported PNG. Export PDF or SVG - and if those are not offered, the figure is being drawn by a GPU renderer, which cannot produce vector. Switch to Qt 2-D. See Vector or raster.

It is cropped differently. The exported figure uses the axis limits, not your current zoom. If the range matters, set the limits.

topics.title: It says this graph is unverified
topics.keywords: unverified warning label red trust use anyway safe should i measured
topics.body:
It means nothing has yet measured whether that engine draws its claim correctly. It does not mean it is known to be wrong, and the engine is not hidden or disabled.

What has been checked: that it renders, that it puts your data on the page, and that it produces a picture no other engine produces.

What has not: that the specific claim it makes is true - that the ranks are in the right order, that the colours follow the value, that the widths carry the totals.

What to do with one. Use it to look at your data freely. Before it goes into anything published, check it the way you would check any unfamiliar tool: feed it something whose answer you already know, and confirm the picture says what it should. That is exactly what verifying an engine consists of.

Currently 0 of 2,122 entries are unverified.

topics.title: A control I was using has disappeared
topics.keywords: missing control gone hidden cannot find panel disappeared where layout lost
topics.body:
Three causes, in order of likelihood.

1. The layout changed. Layouts move and hide panels by design - Zen and Bare have almost no permanent controls. Ctrl+K reaches everything from any layout, and View ▸ Layout is always on the menu. View also has explicit toggles for the toolbar, the controls panel and the workspace bar.

2. This figure has not got that thing. Several panels ask the figure what it has rather than assuming. The Range panel shows a row per axis the engine actually reads - a line chart has two, a pie chart has none - so a missing limits row means this engine has no such axis. Engine-specific settings appear only for the engines that declare them.

3. It needs an add-on. Analysis and literature controls say so rather than vanishing, so if a panel is telling you something is unavailable, that is the answer rather than a missing control.

topics.title: It says restart to finish switching
topics.keywords: restart required renderer switch pending reopen change effect later
topics.body:
You changed the renderer. Which scene graph the application runs on is decided once, at startup, so a renderer chosen now takes effect when GraphVis next opens. The menu offers to restart for you.

Until you do, the figure is still being drawn by the old renderer - which matters most if you switched to Qt 2-D in order to export vector. The export will not be vector until the restart has happened.

Nothing is lost by restarting: figures in a project are still there, and the state of the current figure is carried across.

topics.title: Graph packs
topics.keywords: pack packs core engineering earth life physics enable subset
topics.body:
Packs decide which graphs the library offers. Turning one off does not uninstall anything - it shortens the list, which is the point when you are looking for a box plot among 2,122 entries. Options ▸ Graph packs.

Core (815 entries) — The ordinary chart types, statistics, distributions and model diagnostics. Always on.

topics.title: Axis scales (13)
topics.keywords: scale variant log logarithmic semilog z-score quantile axis transform
topics.body:
Most catalogue entries are one engine at one of these scales. Choosing a scale changes how the axis is marked, not what your data is - nothing on disk is touched and the figure can be put back.

Linear Scale — x: linear, y: linear
Logarithmic Scale — x: log₁₀, y: log₁₀
Semi-Log X — x: log₁₀, y: linear
Semi-Log Y — x: linear, y: log₁₀
Log(1+x) Scale — x: log₁₀(1+x), y: log₁₀(1+x)
Semi-Log(1+x) X — x: log₁₀(1+x), y: linear
Semi-Log(1+x) Y — x: linear, y: log₁₀(1+x)
Standardised (Z-Score) — x: z-score, y: z-score
Z-Score X — x: z-score, y: linear
Z-Score Y — x: linear, y: z-score
Quantile Scale — x: quantile, y: quantile
Quantile X — x: quantile, y: linear
Quantile Y — x: linear, y: quantile

Reading these. A log axis cannot show zero or a negative number, and points at zero simply vanish; log(1+x) exists for exactly that case. A z-score axis is standard deviations from the mean, which is how two columns in different units are compared on one pair of axes. A quantile axis is position in the sorted sample, which is how a column that is mostly one value stops being one pixel wide.

topics.body:

Perceptually Uniform (7)

Scientific Sequential (25)

Which group to use. Perceptually uniform for a quantity you want read off the figure - equal steps in the number are equal steps in the colour, which is what makes a gradient in the picture mean a gradient in the data. Diverging for a quantity with a meaningful middle, such as an anomaly about zero. Categorical for labels, never for numbers. Terrain, ocean and rainbow maps are here because conventions in some fields expect them, not because they read well: Jet in particular invents a bright band in the middle of the range that is not in your data.

topics.title: Window layouts (26)
topics.keywords: layout window arrangement rail inspector zen dock shape interface
topics.body:
View ▸ Layout. A layout rearranges the whole window: which panels exist, where they sit, and whether there is a bar across the top at all. It changes nothing about your data or your figure, so trying one costs nothing.

If a layout hides a control you want, Ctrl+K reaches everything from any layout, and View ▸ Layout is always on the menu.

Rail
A strip of symbols down one edge chooses which single panel is showing. The figure keeps the rest of the window, and a dozen panels cost one narrow strip.
  ▮ Activity rail (after VS Code) — Symbols down the left edge, one panel open at a time, and the data table along the bottom where a table's shape actually fits.
  ◫ Opposed rails (after JupyterLab, VS Code's secondary side bar) — Browse on the left, edit on the right. The graph catalogue and the axis mapping are both visible at once instead of taking turns.
  ⋮▮ Persistent rail (after Obsidian) — The rail stays when the panel is shut, so you can give the figure the whole window and still switch panels without bringing one back.
  ◧ Summoning inspector (after Figma) — The browse side hides itself and the edit side calls itself: click something on the figure and its settings appear on the right.

Tree and inspector
A structure tree on one edge and a properties panel on another, with the figure between them. The shape most scientific software already uses.
  ⌸ Project and log (after Origin) — Project tree on the left, figure in the middle, solver and import messages along the bottom where output belongs.
  ⊟ Object and properties (after Grapher) — The list of things above the settings for the selected thing, both on one edge. The cheapest layout in width, so the figure keeps the most of it.
  ❏ Free docks (after LabPlot, Qt dock widgets) — Nothing is docked. Every panel is a window you put where you want it, including on a second monitor.
  ⊞ Tree and datasets (after Veusz) — Structure and settings on the left, the columns you have loaded on the right, and a row of add-this buttons across the top.

Modes and pages
The whole window changes with the task. The figure stays; everything around it is replaced.
  ▭▭ Pipeline pages (after DaVinci Resolve) — Data, Map, Plot, Analyse, Read, Publish - as pages along the bottom, left to right in the order the work happens. Each page is a different window.
  ⊤ Workspace tabs (after Blender) — Named arrangements as tabs across the top, over panes that tile rather than float. Nothing ever covers the figure.
  ◑ Personas (after Affinity) — The figure stays exactly where it is and the whole toolset around it changes between plotting, fitting and annotating.
  ▬ Ribbon (after Excel, SigmaPlot, Origin) — A band across the top that changes with the task. Everything is visible and nothing is behind a menu, at the cost of the height a figure wants.

Fixed frames
Permanent slots, no docking and no floating. Nothing is ever hidden, so nothing is ever forgotten.
  ▤ Notebook (after Jupyter, Observable) — Several figures stacked as a document, so two graphs can be compared side by side rather than one at a time.
  ⌷ Shelves (after Tableau) — Columns on the left, and the X, Y and Z shelves in a strip above the figure. The mapping is always on screen instead of being a panel you go and visit.
  田 Quadrants (after RStudio) — Four panes, all permanent: figure, data, settings and output. Any one can be blown up to fill the window and dropped back.
  ⊐ Sections (after GraphPad Prism) — Data, Results, Graphs and Layouts as typed sections along the bottom, with a navigator that groups a figure with the table and the fit it came from.
  ◨ Inspector (after Illustrator's Properties panel) — One scrolling column of settings on the right and no tabs at all. Nothing is ever hidden behind another tab, at the cost of scrolling.

Focus
The figure fills the window and the rest is summoned. For reading, presenting and the last look before export.
  ○ Zen (after VS Code Zen mode) — The figure and nothing else. Controls come back on Ctrl+K or by moving to an edge.
  ▯ Centred (after VS Code centred layout) — The figure held to a column in the middle of the window, at the proportions it will have on the page, with margins either side.
  ▤▏ Reader (after Notion, iA Writer) — One list on the left and the document beside it, with nothing else competing. For working through a paper rather than a dataset.
  ⌕ Command bar (after Superhuman, Raycast) — Almost no permanent chrome. The figure gets the whole window and every control is reached by typing for it.

No top bar
The bar of words across the top is gone. Home, Literature, Visualize, Data, Analysis and Publish move to a strip of symbols down one edge, or to Ctrl+K, and the window looks like a different application.
  ◌ Symbols only (after Blender, Krita) — The same arrangement with the words taken out: the top bar becomes a row of symbols about a third the height, and the panel keeps the space it gives up.
  ▌ Left spine (after Slack, Discord) — No bar across the top at all. The six workspaces become a spine of symbols down the left edge, with the panel beside it and the figure filling the rest.
  ▐ Right spine (after Photoshop, Affinity) — The same again on the other edge, for a left-handed pointer or a second screen on the left: workspaces and panels both on the right, figure hard left.
  ▙ Spine and table (after Excel, Tableau) — Workspaces down the left edge, the data table along the bottom, and nothing above the figure - for working between the numbers and the picture.
  □ Bare (after Preview, Quick Look) — Nothing but the figure: no top bar, no spine, no panel. Everything is reached with Ctrl+K, which is the one thing this shape depends on you knowing.

topics.title: Field estimators
topics.keywords: estimator interpolation kriging idw spline loess surface grid field scattered
topics.body:
View ▸ Estimating a field ▸ Method. A contour, surface or heat map needs a value everywhere; measurements exist only where you measured. An estimator is the rule that fills in between, and the choice is a statement about your data, not a preference.

Recommended
  Auto (data-aware)

Structured matrix methods
  Nearest Neighbor
  Bilinear Interpolation
  Bicubic Interpolation
  Rectangular B-Spline
  Monotone PCHIP (Structured)

Unstructured scattered estimators
  Delaunay Triangulation (Linear)
  Natural Neighbor (Sibson's)
  Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW)
  Modified Shepard's Method

Radial basis functions
  Thin Plate Spline (TPS)
  Multiquadric RBF
  Gaussian RBF

Statistical and local regression
  Ordinary Kriging
  Moving Least Squares (MLS)
  LOESS / LOWESS

Auto looks at whether your points fall on a grid and picks accordingly, and is the right answer until you have a reason it is not.

The options beside it.

Beyond the measurements — what happens outside the area you sampled: Mask outside convex hull; Nearest fill outside hull; IDW full-domain extension; Linear + nearest full rectangle; Edge-clamped full rectangle
Values — whether the estimate may exceed what you observed: Allow estimator overshoot; Clamp to observed response range — and the space it is fitted in: Linear values; Log10 values
Kriging variogram — how quickly the response is assumed to decorrelate: Exponential; Spherical; Gaussian
Failed runs — how much of the surface one failure invalidates (Sample cell only; Conservative local region; Voronoi failure region; None (fit through failures)), whether holes are bridged (Preserve all failures; Bridge isolated failures; Bridge small enclosed holes; Bridge all interior holes), and how a masked area is drawn (Transparent; Fallback colour; Nearest Neighbor Fill; Local Mean Imputation; Baseline Clamp (colour-scale minimum); Symmetric Mirror Fill)

The distinction that matters most: masking is honesty and bridging is convenience. A masked area says “not measured”. Anything that fills it in is the program's guess wearing the same colours as your data.

topics.title: Engines with constants of their own
topics.keywords: parameter constant dalitz forest pooled mass setting engine
topics.body:
Almost every engine gets everything it needs from your columns. A few need a number your data cannot supply - a particle mass, or which kind of effect measure a column holds - and those appear as extra controls when the engine is chosen.

Dalitz Plot
  Parent mass [mass] — The decaying particle. Must exceed the three daughters together, or there is no allowed region.
  Daughter 1 [mass] — The particle whose squared mass with daughter 2 is the x axis.
  Daughter 2 [mass] — Shared by both axes: m2(12) on x and m2(23) on y.
  Daughter 3 [mass] — The particle whose squared mass with daughter 2 is the y axis.

Choropleth
  Value scale — 0 linear. 1 log10, for a quantity spanning orders of magnitude - a region whose value is zero or negative is left unfilled, because it has no place on a logarithmic ramp. 2 quantile, which puts an equal number of regions in each class and shows rank rather than magnitude.
  Classes — How many classes quantile classing uses; ignored by the other two scales. Five is the usual cartographic choice - past about nine a reader can no longer tell two classes apart on the map.

Forest Plot
  Pooled estimate — 0 none. 1 for a ratio measure - risk ratio, odds ratio, hazard ratio - with the null at 1. 2 for a difference measure - mean difference, risk difference - with the null at 0. The weighting is inverse-variance either way; the number only chooses where no effect sits, which the data cannot say.

Scatter + Marginals
  Marginals — 0 over the data, translucent, keeping the whole frame for the scatter. 1 in a reserved gutter outside the plot area, which hides nothing and costs the scatter the space it takes.
  Marginal size [% of frame] — How much of the frame each strip spans. About a sixth - 17% - is enough to read a shape and little enough that a strip cannot be mistaken for the data it sits over.

topics.title: Publication profiles (65)
topics.keywords: journal profile publication export dpi width millimetres submit nature science elsevier ieee wiley springer plos
topics.body:
A profile is a figure specification: a column width in millimetres, a text size in points at final size, a minimum line weight and a resolution floor. The figure is re-rendered at those measurements rather than scaled to them, which is the whole point - shrinking a screen figure to 89 mm takes its 8 pt labels down to about 3 pt, and that is what comes back from a copy editor.

Working profiles

Screen (default) — 165 mm wide, 144 dpi, 8 pt text.
  The on-screen look, for working rather than submitting. Switch to a publisher profile before exporting.

Thesis / A4 report — 160 mm wide, 600 dpi, 9 pt text.
  A4 text width less 25 mm margins, at a size that stays readable printed one-up in a bound thesis. Not a publisher standard - a sensible default. University format guides (Pittsburgh, UCSF, Indiana, UNC, ASU) specify page size, margins and a 9-11 pt floor for text inside figures rather than figure widths.

Conference poster (A1) — 250 mm wide, 300 dpi, 24 pt text.

  APA 7: sans-serif figure text 8-14 pt, clear dark labels, restrained decoration. APA specify sufficient resolution rather than one DPI; 300 is a practical baseline. Their own pages refuse automated access, so this is not a directly sourced profile.

Publishers (61)

Every number in these is what that publisher's own author guidelines state. Where a publisher does not publish a figure, the profile's note says so rather than quietly filling one in - a profile that looks authoritative and is not is the one thing here nobody would think to check. topics.title: Colour-vision modes
topics.keywords: colourblind colorblind protanopia deuteranopia tritanopia monochrome accessible
topics.body:
View ▸ Colour vision chooses the palette the series are drawn in. This changes the figure itself, so a figure exported in one of these modes carries that palette wherever it goes.

Standard (safe for all types)
Protanopia (red-blind)
Deuteranopia (green-blind)
Tritanopia (blue-blind)
Monochrome (no colour)

Standard is safe for all three deficiencies and is the right choice unless you are designing for one in particular. A palette tuned for one deficiency is not automatically safe for another - measured true of protanopia and deuteranopia, false of tritanopia - and GraphVis says so on the menu when the one you picked has that problem.

Separately, Preview as this reader sees it simulates the deficiency over the whole figure without changing it. That is a check, not a setting: it shows you what somebody else sees.
